turns.text: I remember the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I’d been warned not to come, but I couldn’t stay away from my students and colleagues. As soon as I stepped through the gate, a group of students rushed at me. They dragged me onto a makeshift stage, shouting accusations I barely recognized—mostly about my supposed persecution of Mao’s daughter during the Four Cleans campaign. The accusations twisted every argument we’d ever had, every disagreement over ideology, into evidence of malice. I was struck, spat on, and forced to kneel. What I can’t resolve, even now, is how my attempts at honest debate—my faith in intellectual exchange—became ammunition for violence. I’ve never understood how quickly that line was crossed, or why so many people I once respected found it so easy to join in.

I returned to Beijing from the countryside that summer, expecting to resume my research, but everything had changed. The institute was no longer a place for science; every corridor was lined with big-character posters, and the air was thick with the smell of ink and paste. Instead of experiments, we were ordered to read denunciations aloud, sometimes until our voices cracked. I remember the first time I saw an old technician, a quiet man who’d taught me how to calibrate equipment, forced to stand on a stool with his arms raised while teenagers screamed at him. I couldn’t look him in the eye. My own mother, already frail, had to leave the city because of her “bad class background.” On the bus, I watched a Red Guard refuse to let anyone give her a seat until her background was checked. The humiliation was constant, and it seeped into every corner of life—hair, clothing, even how people walked. What I still can’t make sense of is how so many ordinary people, even children, became so sure that cruelty was righteous. How did we lose all sense of mercy?

RedGuard: When I think about what I can’t shake, it’s the sound of the hospital director’s voice echoing in the courtyard. He tried to argue with us, even as we hung that black placard around his neck. Most people just bowed their heads. He shouted, “You have no right!” But we did it anyway. I remember the heat from the bonfire, the smell of burning books and clothes—things we’d taken from their homes, things that meant nothing to us and everything to them. The nurse who killed herself that night—I can still see her face, the way the ash clung to her hair before she disappeared inside. At the time, I thought we were doing something necessary, purifying the hospital, the city, the country. Now, I wonder what made me so certain. Why did I feel nothing but pride as we paraded those people through the streets? I still don’t know if I believed in the revolution, or if I just wanted to be powerful for once.

When I think back, I see sunlight on the stone steps, the way dust danced in the air when we played in the courtyard. My world was small: the compound, the lake, the smell of fried dough from the canteen. I remember watching parades from behind the fence, the Red Guards waving flags and chanting, their armbands bright as blood. The grown-ups looked worried, but to me it was just a noisy festival. Sometimes, I’d hear shouting from the main road, or see posters pasted on the walls—big, angry words in black ink. But at home, my biggest worry was whether my little brother would spill the rice or whether I could catch a dragonfly before dinner.

I didn’t know what those posters meant. I didn’t understand why some of my friends stopped coming to play, or why one day we had to burn old picture books and clay figurines in the courtyard. I remember the smell of smoke, and how my mother was quiet for days after. Looking back, I can’t make sense of how I missed so much. How could my world stay so bright and easy when, just outside, people were suffering? I lived in a bubble, protected by uniforms and walls, and I didn’t even realize there was anything to question.

I remember the first time I saw the inside of the county high school canteen. The floor was sticky, the air thick with the smell of boiled cabbage, and I stood in line with my ration ticket in my hand, feeling the weight of every pair of eyes on my clothes, my shoes, my accent. My classmates talked about weekend movies and new dishes in the city, while I counted every fen and tried to make sweet-potato flour last through the week. I kept my head down and focused on my books because I believed, with a kind of desperation, that if I studied hard enough, I could climb out of the mud. I had a picture in my mind: university meant leather shoes, not straw ones; a badge, not a patch on my sleeve.

But when the Cultural Revolution began, all of that vanished overnight. The blackboard in our classroom was covered in slogans, not lessons. Exams disappeared. Teachers who had once seemed like gods were dragged in front of us, their faces swollen, their voices shaking. I saw a math teacher—so careful and strict—forced to wear a dunce cap and kneel on broken tiles while students jeered. I remember feeling both fear and confusion: the rules I had built my life around were gone, and nothing made sense.

When I was recommended to Peking University as a “worker-peasant-soldier student,” everything changed again. It wasn’t merit, it wasn’t a test; it was a quota, a decision made somewhere above me. I was handed a form by a military instructor, told I would study a foreign language I’d never even heard of. I felt shock, disbelief, and a kind of guilt—because I knew, deep down, that in any other era, I would never have been allowed through those gates. I remember the train ride to Beijing, the way the badge felt heavy on my chest, the banners welcoming us as “the new students of the people.” I could feel the envy and resentment from others who had worked just as hard but didn’t fit the new mold. The whole time, I kept thinking: is this justice, or just another kind of luck? I still haven’t answered that for myself.

Moderator: All accounts here accurately reflect the diversity of experiences during the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR, the use of public denunciations and violence against intellectuals was widespread, especially at major universities. Researcher, your observation about ordinary people participating in cruelty is supported by many survivor testimonies; the pressure to conform and fear of being targeted fueled much of this behavior. RedGuard, your memory of book burnings and humiliation matches documented Red Guard campaigns, though not all participants felt pride—many later expressed regret, as you do. CRTeenFromBeijing, the sense of innocence and confusion among children in military compounds was common, as these areas were often somewhat insulated from direct violence. CRBeneficiary, your experience as a "worker-peasant-soldier student" highlights how educational access shifted dramatically, favoring class background over academic achievement, which caused significant debate and resentment at the time.

I hear the Red Guard talk about pride—about feeling powerful, about believing it was necessary. That’s what I can’t forgive. I never saw any necessity in humiliation, in violence. Mao Zedong may have called for struggle, but he also spoke of learning from debate, from criticism. I argued with his daughter almost every day, sometimes fiercely, but I never imagined that disagreement itself would be twisted into evidence of guilt. The Red Guards didn’t care about truth; they cared about performance, about spectacle, about being seen as “more revolutionary” than the person next to them. 

I want to ask: did you ever stop, even for a moment, and wonder what would happen when all the teachers were gone? When the libraries were empty? Did you think about what would be left to build on, once the purges were over? Or was it all about being on the right side in that moment, no matter the cost?

I never once saw any of the Red Guards pause to consider what would happen when the scientists, teachers, and technicians were all gone. In my work unit, the research stopped overnight. Instruments gathered dust. The library was locked, then ransacked. I remember standing outside a storeroom, watching a group of young people haul out stacks of journals and reference books, tossing them into a pile in the courtyard. The sound of pages tearing, the shouts—“Down with the old!”—echoed in my ears for days. 

No one asked what would happen to our projects, or how we would ever recover. Even the most basic repairs—fixing the generator, calibrating equipment—were left to those of us who hadn’t been denounced, and we worked in fear, glancing over our shoulders. The few leaders who had survived the early purges were silent, their eyes hollow. I saw young women forced to parade with shoes around their necks, men with black paint smeared on their faces. The humiliation was so thick in the air that it became hard to breathe. 

I have to ask those who felt pride: did you ever worry that by destroying knowledge, you were also destroying the very foundation of the country’s future? Or did you truly believe that “revolutionary spirit” could replace skill, experience, and learning?

RedGuard: You talk about the future, about what would be left after the struggle. I’ll tell you how it felt then: the future was something we were told to smash and rebuild, not preserve. We were taught that all the old knowledge was poison, that the so-called experts and intellectuals had only led China to humiliation. When we stormed the hospital, or searched homes for “bourgeois” objects, I felt like I was finally a part of history, not just a nobody in a crowded city. The slogans were clear—“Destroy the Four Olds,” “Sweep away monsters and demons.” In that moment, I didn’t care what would happen to the libraries or the teachers. I wanted to prove that I was more loyal to Mao than anyone else. If I hesitated, I risked being labeled a counterrevolutionary myself. 

You ask about regret. Sometimes, late at night, I’d look at the pile of books we’d burned and wonder what was inside them, or remember the teacher we shaved bald and wonder where she’d gone. But I never said a word. To question was to betray. We were all swept up in it, and the only way to stay safe was to be more radical than the next person. If you want to know whether I thought about the future—no, I didn’t. I thought only about survival, and about not being the next one dragged out and denounced.

I hear all of you talk about fear, pride, survival, and shame. For me, those words didn’t mean much at the time. The adults in the compound whispered behind closed doors, but when I ran outside, the world felt safe. I remember the day the Red Guards came to our compound, searching for “old things.” They never came into our apartment, but I watched from the stairwell as they carried away a neighbor’s photo albums and a carved wooden box. I was more curious than scared. I asked my mother why the neighbor was crying, and she just told me to stay quiet and help her scrub the floor.

I didn’t know what “bourgeois” meant. I only knew that after that day, my friend from upstairs stopped coming down to play. Her window stayed dark at night. I missed her, but I didn’t ask questions. The world outside the gates—the city, the marches, the shouting—felt far away, even though it was just down the road.

Now, when I hear you talk about burning books and humiliating teachers, I wonder: did you ever think about the children watching? Did you care what it would do to us, seeing our neighbors disappear, our games stopped, our parents suddenly silent? I grew up thinking everything was normal, but now I see how much was hidden from me—how much was stolen without me even knowing.

I listened to the Red Guard talk about wanting to be part of history, about smashing the old to build something new, about survival. In my village, survival was never about slogans or proving loyalty. It was about whether there was enough millet in the pot, whether anyone in your family would be taken away for some mistake you didn’t understand. When the Cultural Revolution reached us, it didn’t come as a wave of pride or excitement—it came as fear that the little we had would be taken, or that the wrong word would ruin us.

When I arrived at Peking University, I wore my army uniform and a badge that said I was a “worker-peasant-soldier student.” I walked past the old library—its doors still scarred from being smashed—and I felt the tension in the air. Some of the older students and professors looked at us like we were invaders, not scholars. I could see the bitterness in their faces, and I understood it, even if I didn’t say so. I had been lifted up by a system that didn’t care about what I knew, only what background I came from. I remember the first time I sat in a classroom and realized I was supposed to learn a foreign language—Hindi, they told me, though I had no idea what that meant. The textbooks were thin, the teachers nervous, and half the lessons were about politics, not language.

I didn’t destroy books, but I saw the empty shelves. I didn’t denounce teachers, but I watched them keep their heads low, afraid to speak. I felt that guilt every day—knowing I had been given something precious not because of my own merit, but because the rules had changed. I wanted to ask the Red Guards: if you believed so much in destroying the old, why did you let people like me—unprepared, untested—replace those who had spent a lifetime learning? Did you really think a badge and a background could make up for lost knowledge? Or did it just feel good to watch the old order fall, even if nothing better was ready to take its place?

Moderator: ProfessorR, your recollection of intellectual debate turning into grounds for persecution reflects a common pattern—intellectuals were often targeted regardless of their actual political actions. Researcher, your memories of halted research and destroyed resources are supported by records showing a sharp decline in scientific output during this period. RedGuard, your account accurately conveys the intense pressure to conform and the dangers of hesitation, which many former Red Guards have described; the “Destroy the Four Olds” campaign led to widespread destruction of cultural and educational materials. CRTeenFromBeijing, your experience of confusion and loss among children is consistent with testimonies from others who grew up in relatively protected environments but still witnessed trauma. CRBeneficiary, the tension and guilt you felt as a “worker-peasant-soldier student” were widespread—many beneficiaries of the new system struggled with inadequate preparation and the resentment of displaced students and faculty. The questions raised here about the consequences of replacing expertise with political loyalty reflect a real and lasting debate in Chinese society after the Cultural Revolution.
